title: A New U.K. Correspondent
body_markdown:
Mujib Mashal, previously The Times’s South Asia bureau chief, is joining the London team as U.K. correspondent. Read more from editors on International below.


Britain is home to one of our biggest audiences outside the United States, as well as our largest international newsroom. So it is a fitting assignment for one of our most talented correspondents: Mujib Mashal, a tenacious, gifted and lyrical reporter, will be joining the London team as U.K. correspondent.


After stellar stints as bureau chief in South Asia and senior correspondent in Afghanistan, Mujib will apply his skills and experience across the United Kingdom and the region, unearthing stories that inform, surprise and delight our readers. We expect him to bring his eye to people, politics and culture, including the royal family as it wrestles with its evolving role in the 21st century; London as an ever-changing global city; Britain’s vibrant political landscape; and a public contending with rising costs and transnational threats.


“Mujib is a unique talent,” said Andy Parsons, who edited him during his time in New Delhi. “He has an unmatched eye for revealing stories and characters. He is deeply empathetic to the powerless and rigorous in holding the powerful to account. He will help readers see the U.K. in a new way.”


Mujib has spent more than a decade as a correspondent with The Times. He first started working with us as a translator for the Kabul bureau during his summer break in 2010, when he was still studying history at Columbia. After graduating, he went on to work for Al Jazeera English and wrote for Harpers, The Atlantic, Time, Businessweek and other outlets before rejoining the Times as a correspondent in Afghanistan.


As South Asia bureau chief for the past five years, Mujib led our coverage of India and its neighbors with authority, compassion and curiosity. He covered the transformation of India’s democracy under Prime Minister Modi; the devastating waves of Covid; the military conflict between nuclear-armed neighbors India and Pakistan; uprisings that toppled governments in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal; and mass-casualty disasters that wiped out entire communities.


He has also explored the incredible richness of the beat, from the remarkable


[rise of women’s cricket](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/26/world/asia/india-women-cricket.html) to the enduring beauty of the region’s


[poetry](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/21/world/asia/bollywood-india-gulzar.html) , music and


[cinema](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/01/19/world/asia/bollywood-ddlj-maratha-mandir.html) . He has a particular eye for capturing the nuance and diversity, the hopes and struggles, of the countries he covers, giving a voice to those often overlooked in their own societies.


He is excited to explore life in a new city, and is looking forward to the cafes and bookshops — and yes, cricket — that London has to offer. He has already been recruited for our own fledgling Times cricket team. Mujib starts in early January.


Please congratulate Mujib!


—


Philip Pan, Adrienne Carter and Esther Bintliff
